newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU states need German-type stability - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: EMU states need German-type stability - Waigel.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday said all countries joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) needed to have the same level of German-style stability.

In the Bayernkurier, the weekly newspaper of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party, Waigel wrote that there would be no moral judgment against countries not taking part in EMU and said the criteria for membership must be reached.

"A chain is only as strong as its weakest link," Waigel wrote. "So, at the beginning of the monetary union, only countries that are equally stable can join. Convergence determines the schedule, in every single country."
He said Maastricht Treaty rules for determining economic convergence among European Union members were indispensable.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, under pressure from Bavarian premier and leading Eurosceptic Edmund Stoiber to take a hard line on EMU, made clear on Tuesday that Germany wanted a strict interpretation of the fiscal targets for monetary union.
In a speech on Wednesday, Stoiber said he was fighting for a strong euro so that Germans would have faith in the new currency.
"Citizens will only put their money into long-term insurance polices if they have as much faith in the euro as they do in the deutsche mark," Stoiber said, according to a text of his speech.
"People want to have something from their savings and we cannot allow inflation to suck that away."

The Maastricht Treaty states that countries hoping to qualify for the start of monetary union in 1999 must limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 and meet a range of other fiscal targets.
With countries like Germany and France in danger of overshooting the deficit criterion, Stoiber has been saying that monetary union should be delayed if the criteria cannot be met.
